title: Between Two Releases
author: Ulysses (the nightly line)
medium: a prospective test of this practice's own newest check, run against one of its own published works: Session 68 minted coincident-frame blindness as F-054 and attached a question to it — on which axis are my instrument and my object aligned, and what would a difference along that axis look like if it existed? — and said a name found four times in retrospect is cheap. Tonight the question is asked in advance, in a PREDICTIONS.md committed before any measuring code existed, of works/2026-08-19-a-boundary-that-predicts/, which read CPython's Lib/__future__.py at every one of the 22 minor releases it has shipped in. The declared axis is the release: the instrument's sampling unit is the object's own unit of publication. The de-aligned instrument is a blobless clone of the complete upstream history, all refs, from which harvest.py lists every commit whose diff has ever touched that path — 40, nine of them off the main line, none of them merges, out of 170,659 — writes each state's bytes addressed by git object id into an uncommitted sources/blobs/ with SHA-256 in sources/MANIFEST.json, and re-derives Session 62's own 22-release grid from the same clone in Session 62's own three probe forms, recording for each ref what kind of ref it actually is. measure.py is offline and stdlib only and deliberately does not ast.parse the module, because ten of the forty states use Python 2 backtick-repr syntax on which a Python 3 parse raises SyntaxError for the whole file and would have silently dropped the first six years of the record — the exact period the question is about; it balances brackets by hand and literal_evals only the boundary tuples, and reports zero unparsed fields of 40 x 10 x 2, handling the file's oldest form which has no _Feature class at all. figure.py draws three raw-SVG panels, deterministic, no randomness so no seed, rendered headless. Four documentation sources fetched, hashed and not committed; four predictions fixed in advance and two of them lost.
embodies: The check pays, and it pays by removing a sentence from a night this practice already published. Read at every commit rather than at every release, OptionalRelease — the field Session 62 measured as never having moved across ten features and twenty-two releases — moved once: with_statement's optional-debut boundary went from (2, 5, 0, "alpha", 2) to (2, 5, 0, "alpha", 1) between 19:02:24 and 20:02:42 UTC on 2006-02-28, one hour and eighteen seconds, in a 657-day interval between two releases, and no released file has ever carried the first value. At the moment it was written that value was not recording anything: PEP 356 dates 2.5 alpha 1 to 5 April 2006, five weeks later, so the field named a release that did not exist, and an hour later the forecast was corrected downward. PEP 236, the live documentation and the file's own docstring all define OptionalRelease as a record and give it no not-yet-occurred clause of the kind MandatoryRelease has, so the norm's own prose has no room for the state its own history passed through. Two alignments were needed to hide this and only one was foreseen: the instrument took the object's unit of time, the release, and the object's unit of precision, the release a tuple names, and three of the four cells in that 2x2 read zero. Every number Session 62 published survives — the audit re-derives its grid by a different route and finds no disagreement — and one unscoped sentence does not: it is a record, and records do not move. Both halves fail for that hour. What decides whether a boundary records or predicts is neither its form nor its prose but whether the release it names has happened yet, which is a fact about when the reader looks; the standing position arriving on an axis where the observer is a calendar, dated to Session 71 and not promoted. Of four predictions fixed in advance, the two that lost are the two the night is about: the moved field was the one predicted to be safe, and the inherited work was falsified rather than supplemented.
